reviewer.summary: The report addresses all nine planned claims, and its main estimates match the cited final-stage findings. It appropriately limits the conclusions to the eligible Columbia-linked works and distinguishes inconclusive results from evidence of no association. Before release, correct the descriptions of citation eligibility and count validation so readers can tell exactly which works entered each analysis and what the audit verified.

issues.problem: The sentence “The index also had to show evidence of a citation: a positive total, a positive count in a later calendar year through the cutoff year, or a citing work dated after publication” omits that the dated-work check used the local snapshot. The next sentence presents direct citation within the window as a requirement for the entire analysis, and the reference appendix labels all 8,000 draws “No citation requirement,” even though every draw passed the initial citation-evidence screen.
issues.fix: Specify that the dated citing work was identified in the local snapshot. Replace “The analysis used a stricter rule” with “The primary disruption analyses additionally required a direct citation within the relevant window.” Rename the appendix column “All sampled works (no additional window-based citation filter).”

issues.problem: “Counts by year agreed with direct totals or counts from citing works’ own references in all 62 checks” describes all 62 validations as checks of annual counts. T15 includes main- and short-window totals as well as other grouped-count comparisons.
issues.fix: Replace the sentence with “All 62 grouped-count checks, including checks of totals over the main and short windows, agreed with independent counts or classifications based on citing works’ reference lists.”

issues.problem: After “Fourteen of 20 fields pointed to a decline,” the sentence “Those fields together contained 6,074 works” could attribute the count to the 14 negative-slope fields. F14 gives the count for all 20 qualifying fields.
issues.fix: Change the sentence to “Across all 20 qualifying fields, the analysis included 6,074 works.”

issues.problem: “For the top tenth, the estimated change was 2.73 points more positive than for the least-cited half, suggesting a weaker decline at the top” makes the top-group point estimate sound negative. It was slightly positive, although its interval was wide.
issues.fix: State that the top-group estimate was a rise of 0.23 rank points per doubling, with a 95% interval from a 4.33-point decline to a 3.37-point rise. Retain the direct contrast and its interval to show that neither a reversal nor a steeper decline at the top was established.

issues.problem: “Including uncited works whose references were cited” can be read as saying these works had never been cited, rather than that no direct citation was observed within the relevant window.
issues.fix: Use “Including works whose references were cited but that received no direct citation within the relevant window.”

reader.summary: The main story is easy to follow, and the worked example makes the disruption score concrete. The main gaps are how works with several authors enter the within-author comparison, how citation groups are defined, and what the model for highly cited references assumes.

issues.problem: “We fitted a trend allowing each author, publication year and main OpenAlex topic to have a different average rank.” This does not tell readers how a work with several qualifying authors enters the comparison.
issues.fix: A work entered the comparison once for each qualifying author, with its sampling weight split among them. We estimated how rank changed with team size while allowing average ranks to differ by author, publication year and the main topic assigned by OpenAlex.

issues.problem: “Within each publication year, citation ranks below 50 form the least-cited group. The middle group starts at 50 and the top group at 90.” Readers have not been told that these are percentiles, not citation counts or places in an ordered list.
issues.fix: Within each publication year, we ranked works by their citation counts on a percentile scale from 0 to 100. The least-cited group was below the 50th percentile. The middle group began at the 50th percentile, and the top group began at the 90th.

issues.problem: “For references with at least 50 citations, we could not tell whether higher counts became rarer at different rates.” The text explains the model for reference age but not what a rate of decline means for citation counts.
issues.fix: The citation model assumed that each doubling of the citation count reduced the predicted frequency by the same fraction. Among references with at least 50 citations, we could not tell whether that fraction differed by team size.

issues.problem: “The estimated change in rank per doubling was 4.26 points more positive for works with an acknowledgment than for works without one.” The contrast alone leaves readers guessing whether ranks fell in both groups or moved in opposite directions.
issues.fix: For each doubling of team size, disruption rank fell by an estimated 3.75 points for works without a recorded acknowledgment and rose by an estimated 0.52 points for works with one. The estimated change was 4.26 points higher for works with an acknowledgment.

issues.problem: “Including uncited works whose references were cited, which score zero, barely changed the main team-size result but changed the short-window estimate and the review comparison, as the appendix shows.” Readers must go to the appendix to find out what changed.
issues.fix: Giving a score of zero to works whose references were cited but that were not themselves cited made little difference to the overall result. The estimated decline was steeper in the shorter window, but the two windows still did not clearly differ. The interval for the difference between articles and reviews only just ruled out no difference.

issues.problem: “The index also had to show evidence of a citation: a positive total, a positive count in a later calendar year through the cutoff year, or a citing work dated after publication.” The cutoff year has not yet been given, and “a positive count” makes the entry rule harder to scan.
issues.fix: To enter the sampling list, a work needed at least one citation in its OpenAlex total, at least one citation recorded in a calendar year after publication through 2026, or a record of a citing work published after it.

issues.problem: “The rank, on a scale from 0 to 100, counts the weighted share below the score plus half the weighted share tied with it.” A share may be read as a fraction rather than a percentage, and “counts” makes the calculation harder to follow.
issues.fix: To get the rank on a scale from 0 to 100, add the percentage of eligible works from the same year with lower scores to half the percentage with the same score. Use the sampling weights for both percentages.

issues.problem: “We compared average shares as if groups had the same mix of publication years and quarters. On that measure, works with negative scores were 2.14 percentage points ahead of works with positive scores, with a 95% interval of 1.04 to 3.19 points among 5,421 works.” “Ahead” makes readers look back to recover which share was larger.
issues.fix: We compared the groups as if they had the same mix of publication years and three-month periods within each year. Works with negative disruption scores received a 2.14 percentage point larger share of their citations in the year they were published than works with positive scores did. The 95% interval was 1.04 to 3.19 points, based on 5,421 works.

issues.problem: “Their works also more often scored below zero: more later publications cited the work alongside at least one reference from its own list than cited it without any of its references.” The sentence switches from a group result to the rule for one work, and “its own list” has an unclear referent.
issues.fix: A larger share of works by larger teams scored below zero. For each work with a negative score, more later publications cited both the work and at least one of its references than cited the work without citing any of those references.

issues.problem: “The comparisons within authors instead estimate uncertainty without repeat draws, allowing records that share an author or a work to be related.” “Records” is unexplained here and hides why the observations can be related.
issues.fix: For comparisons within authors, we calculated intervals without drawing new samples. We allowed for the fact that several works can share an author and that one work can enter the comparison under several authors.

issues.problem: “The decline held within authors and in works OpenAlex labelled as articles. Reviews, which OpenAlex labels separately, did not show a clear decline. The main comparison also did not establish a difference between reviews and articles.” This can read as though the article and review results came from the same within-author analysis.
issues.fix: The decline held within authors. In a separate comparison by publication type, disruption rank fell with team size for works OpenAlex classified as articles. The estimate for reviews was uncertain, and the direct comparison did not establish that the trends differed.

reviewer.summary: All nine planned claims have clear statuses, and the report generally distinguishes local agreement, inconclusive results, and claims the data cannot test. The headline estimates checked against F11–F20 match to rounding. Before release, correct the paired-window sample labels and describe the timing result as a mean of within-work shares. The supplied artifact extract ends at T29, so details available only in later artifacts, such as the exact reference-model fit gaps, could not be independently verified.

issues.problem: The appendix rows “Main trend: works cited in both windows” and “Short trend: works cited in both windows” mislabel the 4,721-work sensitivity sample. That sample includes works whose references, but not the focal work itself, were cited in a window. The count for focal works cited in both windows is 4,405 (F18).
issues.fix: Rename both rows to “Main trend: same works eligible in both windows” and “Short trend: same works eligible in both windows.” State that eligibility requires a focal citation in the primary column and a citation to the focal work or at least one reference in the sensitivity column. Note that the simpler ratio still requires a focal citation, which is why its count is unchanged.

issues.problem: “A larger share of the biggest teams’ early citations arrived in the first full year than for solo works” reads as a comparison of pooled citations. F16 estimates the weighted average of individual works’ citation shares, conditional on receiving at least one citation in the two full calendar years.
issues.fix: Replace the summary sentence with: “Among works cited in either of the first two full calendar years after publication, teams of 51–100 authors had a higher average first-year citation share than solo authors.” Use the same distinction in the timing conclusion and summary table.

issues.problem: “The spread of scores differed by team size” can be read as a claim about dispersion. The reported below-zero and cumulative-curve contrasts establish a distributional difference, not specifically a change in dispersion (F12).
issues.fix: Use “The distribution of scores differed by team size” in the summary, C2 conclusion, and comparison table.

issues.problem: “A percentile rank compares the raw score with scores for eligible works from the same year” explains the local method but does not explicitly flag that its ranking population differs from the study’s.
issues.fix: Add: “The original study ranked disruption against all works in its ranking population; we instead calculated sampling-weighted ranks separately within each publication year.”

issues.problem: “References in ten-author works were 5.20 years newer than in solo works” does not identify the focal-cited subset in the body text. F15 separately identifies the all-draw estimate as the original C5 target.
issues.fix: Specify that the 5.20-year difference is a comparison of average reference ages per work in the focal-cited subset. Give the all-draw comparison alongside it: 5.38 years newer, with a 95% interval of 4.58 to 6.24 years, among 1,249 works.

issues.problem: “The review–article interval just ruled out no difference” overstates what a narrowly nonzero sensitivity interval establishes. The primary interval includes zero (F17).
issues.fix: Say: “The nominal 95% interval for the review-minus-article slope difference narrowly excluded zero under the references-only sensitivity rule, but included zero under the primary rule.”

reader.summary: The main findings are easy to follow, and the worked example makes the disruption score concrete. The main revisions are to state who entered the shorter follow-up analysis and what the reference models predict. A few shorter rewrites would make the eligibility rules and comparisons easier to read on the first pass.

issues.problem: “For works from 2024 the shorter window had not ended. We applied the citation rule separately in each window.” This leaves open whether works from 2024 were excluded from the shorter-window analysis or included with incomplete follow-up.
issues.fix: We excluded works from 2024 from the shorter-window analysis because their follow-up was not yet complete. In each window, we included only works that were themselves cited during that window.

issues.problem: “As in the original study, we modelled the share of older references as falling by the same fraction each year. The fitted drop was faster for ten-author than solo works. The citation model assumes the predicted frequency falls by the same fraction each time the citation count doubles. For references with at least 50 citations, we could not tell whether that fraction differed by team size.” It is unclear what “predicted frequency” counts, and “each year” can sound like a change over calendar time rather than a change in the age cutoff.
issues.fix: As in the original study, the age model assumes that raising the age cutoff by one year reduces the share of references older than the cutoff by the same fraction each time. The fitted share fell faster for ten-author works than for solo works. Among references with at least 50 citations, the citation model assumes that the share with a given citation count falls by the same fraction whenever that count doubles. We could not tell whether that fraction differed by team size.

issues.problem: “Our local copy of OpenAlex also needed to show a citation in the total count, in a later calendar year through 2026, or in a record for a work published later.” The three ways of meeting the initial citation rule take a second reading, especially because the last “work” is not identified as the citing work.
issues.fix: To enter the sampling list, a work also needed at least one sign of being cited in our copy of OpenAlex: a positive total citation count, a positive count for a calendar year after publication through 2026, or a record of a citing work published after it.

issues.problem: “Admitting works that scored zero because only their references were cited within the window barely changed the main result, though the short-window estimate was more negative and the review–article interval just ruled out no difference.” This gives exceptions for two comparisons before the reader knows what either comparison measures. “Just ruled out no difference” also takes a second reading.
issues.fix: Move this to the end of the results: “Including works that scored zero because only their references were cited barely changed the main result. In the shorter window, the estimated decline was steeper. The confidence interval for the difference between the trends for reviews and articles narrowly excluded zero.”

issues.problem: “Subtract those that cite the paper alongside at least one reference. Divide by all works citing either the paper or any of its references, counting each once.” The reader has to infer what number is subtracted and whether “either” includes works that cite both. The example clears this up, but the definition can do so directly.
issues.fix: Subtract the number of later works that cite the sampled work together with at least one of its references. Divide the result by the number that cite the sampled work, any of its references, or both. Count each later work only once.

issues.problem: “The middle 95% gives the confidence interval for one estimate, not a whole curve or a difference between plotted points.” The text does not say explicitly what the middle 95% is taken from.
issues.fix: We use the middle 95% of the recalculated values as the confidence interval. It shows uncertainty in one estimate, not in the whole curve or in the difference between points.

issues.problem: “Fourteen of 20 fields pointed to a decline, or 70%, with a 95% interval of 55% to 80%.” “Pointed to a decline” could mean there was clear evidence of a decline in each field, rather than that the estimate was downward.
issues.fix: The estimated trend was downward in 14 of 20 fields. That is 70%, with a 95% confidence interval of 55% to 80% for the share of fields.

issues.problem: “On the same 4,107 works, the decline per doubling was 1.85 points allowing for those differences, with a 95% interval of 0.27 to 3.43 points of decline. Without allowing for them, it was 1.73 points, with an interval of 0.46 to 3.01 points of decline.” “The same” appears before both estimates have been introduced, and “those differences” and “them” make the reader look back to see what each estimate accounts for.
issues.fix: Among 4,107 works, disruption rank fell by 1.85 points per doubling of team size after accounting for author, publication year and topic. The 95% interval was 0.27 to 3.43 points of decline. For the same works without those adjustments, the decline was 1.73 points per doubling, with an interval of 0.46 to 3.01 points of decline.

issues.problem: “The second measure asks what share arrived in the publication year out of all citations through the second full year. We compared groups as if they had the same mix of years and three-month periods within each year.” It takes a second reading to distinguish when the works were published from when their citations arrived.
issues.fix: We also calculated the share of citations that arrived in the publication year, counting citations through the end of the second full calendar year after publication. We compared the groups as if their works had been published in the same mix of years and three-month periods.

issues.problem: “The link with disruption also held within authors and with a shorter window or simpler score.” In the summary, the reader has to reconstruct the direction of the link and what “within authors” means.
issues.fix: Larger teams still showed less disruption when we compared works by the same authors, counted citations over a shorter period, or used a simpler score.

issues.problem: “The count checks show agreement where tested, not complete citation coverage.” The main text does not say what agreed with what.
issues.fix: Our citation counts matched separate counts in the cases we checked, but that does not show that OpenAlex recorded every citation.

reviewer.summary: The report addresses all nine planned claims and clearly separates the local findings from the original study’s broader conclusions. The headline estimates match the cited later-stage findings, and the report discloses nonmonotonic results, inconclusive contrasts and limits on causal interpretation. Before release, correct the description of reference-citation vintages and supply or remove the exact appendix and fit diagnostics that cannot be verified from the supplied evidence.

issues.problem: The exact fit diagnostics in “the largest predicted versus observed gap was 8.1 percentage points for age, using 34,531 references from 624 works” and “For citation counts it was 8.8 points, using 26,259 references from 620 works” cannot be verified from the supplied evidence. F15 supports imperfect fits, but does not give those gaps or denominators, and the cited T76 and T77 rows are not visible. The appendix row “Same trend, bootstrap bounds [T80]” likewise cannot be checked against F17, which gives clustered bounds for that estimate.
issues.fix: Supply the cited artifact rows for the fit diagnostics and bootstrap bounds. If they are unavailable, replace the fit-gap sentences with “Both models fit imperfectly” and omit the separate bootstrap-bounds row, retaining the verified clustered intervals.

issues.problem: “Citations to references were counted when we collected the data” implies that the totals share a collection-date vintage. T10 identifies snapshot-vintage totals for locally matched references, while T11 distinguishes snapshot from live totals.
issues.fix: Replace the sentence with “Reference popularity was measured using cumulative OpenAlex citation totals from the local snapshot or the live index, not citation totals as of the date the focal work was published.”

issues.problem: “The middle 95% of the recalculated estimates forms the confidence interval for a single estimate” does not explain how the bootstrap differs from the sampling design. The appendix discloses that even the fully enumerated 51–100-author stratum was resampled, but leaves the implication unstated.
issues.fix: Call these percentile bootstrap intervals and add that the resampling did not apply a finite-population correction for the original without-replacement design, including for the fully enumerated stratum.

issues.problem: The C9 label “Not testable as stated” is defensible for the original claims, but makes the planned local acknowledgment comparison look untested even though the report presents it.
issues.fix: Use “Partly testable: we compared works by recorded acknowledgment status, not verified funding status. Historical team growth, company patents and Nobel-winning work were not testable.” Apply the same distinction in the summary table.

reader.summary: The main story is easy to follow, and the worked example makes the disruption score concrete. The report needs clearer wording about which works enter each analysis, what they are ranked against, and what the author and reference comparisons estimate.

issues.problem: “The main disruption analyses required a citation to the work itself in each window considered separately.” This can sound as though a work had to be cited in both periods to enter either analysis.
issues.fix: For each citation period, we included a work in the main disruption analysis only if at least one later work cited it during that period.

issues.problem: “We ranked scores against eligible works from the same publication year.” This does not say whether the comparison is with other sampled works or with all eligible works in OpenAlex.
issues.fix: We ranked each work’s score against those of other sampled works from the same publication year that qualified for that analysis.

issues.problem: “A work entered once per qualifying author, with its weight split among them. Among 4,107 works, rank fell by 1.85 points per doubling after accounting for author, year and main OpenAlex topic.” The passage does not clearly distinguish the comparison within authors from the adjustments for year and topic.
issues.fix: We counted each work under every author who met the affiliation rule and divided its sampling weight among them. We compared works by the same author while allowing typical ranks to differ by publication year and main OpenAlex topic. Across 4,107 works, each doubling of team size was associated with a disruption rank 1.85 points lower.

issues.problem: “The citation model assumes the share with a given count falls by the same fraction whenever that count doubles.” After the explanation of the age model, which uses shares above a cutoff, it is unclear whether this means references with exactly a given citation count or references at or above that count.
issues.fix: The model assumes that doubling the citation count reduces the predicted share of references with exactly that count by the same fraction each time.

issues.problem: “Including works that scored zero because only their references were cited in the relevant window barely changed the main result, though the short-window decline was steeper and the interval for the difference between the review and article trends narrowly excluded zero only under this broader rule.” The sentence interrupts the funding discussion, and it is unclear what the shorter-period decline was steeper than.
issues.fix: Move each comparison to the section it concerns. The main result changed little when we also included works whose references were cited but that were not themselves cited. These works scored zero. With them included, the estimated decline was steeper in the shorter period than in the main period, but the difference was uncertain. The interval for the difference between review and article trends just excluded zero under this rule, but not under the main rule.

issues.problem: “More of their works scored below zero: for each such work, more later publications cited it alongside at least one reference than without any of its references.” “More” can mean a larger count rather than a larger share, and “at least one reference” could be any reference.
issues.fix: A larger share of works by larger teams scored below zero. For each of those works, more later publications cited the work together with at least one of its references than cited it without any of them.

issues.problem: “Among works cited in either of the first two full calendar years, teams of 51 to 100 authors had a higher average first-year citation share than solo authors.” The summary does not say what total the first-year share is taken from.
issues.fix: Among works cited in the first two full calendar years after publication, works by teams of 51 to 100 authors received a larger share of those citations in the first year, on average, than solo works did.

issues.problem: “We compared the groups as if they had the same mix of publication years and quarters.” The reader does not yet know which groups are being compared.
issues.fix: We compared works with negative and positive disruption scores as if both groups had the same mix of publication years and quarters.

issues.problem: “Our local copy of OpenAlex also had to show evidence of citation: a positive total, a positive count for a later calendar year through 2026, or a record of a citing work published after the sampled work.” The reader has to supply what the total and count refer to and what “later” is measured from.
issues.fix: Our copy of OpenAlex had to show at least one citation in the work’s overall count or in a calendar year after publication through 2026, or list a citing work published after the sampled work.

issues.problem: “We fitted a line across works with one to ten authors on a scale where each doubling is one step.” The reader has to infer what is doubling and what the line estimates.
issues.fix: For works with one to ten authors, we fitted a trend that estimates the same change in disruption rank for each doubling of team size.

issues.problem: “The within-author intervals use no repeat draws. They allow for several works sharing an author and one work entering under several authors.” This appears before the author comparison is explained, and “no repeat draws” can sound like drawing without replacement rather than using a different way to calculate uncertainty.
issues.fix: Move this to the author comparison: We calculated these intervals without resampling, allowing for several works by the same author and for the same work to be counted under several authors.

issues.problem: “The change per doubling was 2.73 points more positive in the top tenth than in the least-cited half. The 95% interval, from 1.89 points more negative to 6.00 points more positive among 3,734 works, did not establish which group had the steeper decline.” The shifts between “more positive” and “more negative” make the comparison harder to track.
issues.fix: For each doubling of team size, the estimated change in disruption rank was 2.73 points higher in the most-cited tenth than in the least-cited half. The 95% interval, based on 3,734 works, ranged from 1.89 points lower to 6.00 points higher, so we could not tell which group had the steeper decline.

reviewer.summary: The report addresses all nine planned claims, and its headline estimates, intervals, and sample counts match the cited final findings. It distinguishes the locally reproduced patterns from inconclusive results and claims the data cannot test. The remaining edits would make the scope of several comparisons clearer without changing the conclusions.

issues.problem: “For reviews the estimate was unclear, and the comparison did not establish that the trends differed.” This accurately describes the primary analysis, but the sentence does not name that restriction. In the appendix, the review–article contrast excludes zero when references-only cases are included, even though the review trend itself remains inconclusive.
issues.fix: Write: “The review trend was inconclusive under both eligibility rules. The review–article contrast included zero in the primary analysis but narrowly excluded zero when references-only cases were admitted.”

issues.problem: “That means more later publications cited each work alongside at least one of its references than cited it without any of them.” In the summary, “each work” could be read as referring to every larger-team work rather than only to works with negative scores.
issues.fix: Begin the sentence with “For a work that scored below zero,” to make the condition explicit.

issues.problem: “They cited newer and generally more cited sources.” The summary leaves the comparison implicit, while the reported reference contrasts compare ten-author works with solo works.
issues.fix: Write: “Ten-author works cited newer and, on average, more highly cited sources than solo works, using cumulative OpenAlex citation totals.”

reader.summary: The main findings are easy to follow once the measures are defined. Clarify which works entered the sample, where later citations were counted, and how the same-author comparison worked. A few results also need to name the comparison directly rather than sending readers back to an earlier paragraph or the appendix.

issues.problem: “The sampling list required a link to a reference other than the work itself. Our copy of OpenAlex also had to show at least one citation in the work’s total, one in a calendar year after publication through 2026, or a citing work published after the sampled work.” The second sentence makes it hard to tell which of the three citation records is enough to qualify.
issues.fix: To enter the sampling list, a work needed a recorded link to a reference other than itself. It also needed one of three signs of being cited in our copy of OpenAlex: a positive total citation count, a citation recorded in any calendar year from the year after publication through 2026, or a recorded citing work published after it.

issues.problem: “We counted citing works published after the sampled work.” The main text does not say whether the search covered all of OpenAlex or only the Columbia sample. That matters for interpreting the disruption score.
issues.fix: We searched all of OpenAlex, not just the Columbia sample, for works published after the sampled work that cited it, at least one of its references, or both.

issues.problem: “Authors needed a recorded Columbia affiliation on eligible works of different sizes. We counted each work under every author who qualified, splitting its sampling weight among them. We compared works by the same author while letting average ranks differ by year and main OpenAlex topic.” It takes a reread to see who qualified, what was compared for each author, and whether the works had to match by year and topic.
issues.fix: Authors qualified if they had a recorded Columbia affiliation on eligible works with different numbers of authors. We split each work’s sampling weight among its qualifying authors. For each author, we compared disruption ranks for their works on larger and smaller teams, allowing average ranks to differ by publication year and by the main topic OpenAlex assigned to each work.

issues.problem: “A larger share of their works scored below zero. That means more later publications cited each work alongside at least one of its references than cited it without any of them.” The words “each work” can be read as referring to every work by a larger team.
issues.fix: Works by larger teams more often scored below zero. For a work with a score below zero, more later publications cited it with at least one of its references than cited it without any of them.

issues.problem: “On the scale from 0 to 100, add the percentage with lower scores to half the percentage tied, using sampling weights for both. If weights total 100, with 40 below and 20 tied, the rank is 50.” In the example, “40 below and 20 tied” can sound like counts of works rather than shares of the total weight.
issues.fix: The rank runs from 0 to 100. Add the weighted percentage of same-year works with lower scores to half the weighted percentage with the same score. If the total weight is 100, lower scores account for 40 of that weight, and tied scores account for 20, the rank is 50.

issues.problem: “The middle 95% of the recalculated values gives the confidence interval for one estimate. We did not narrow intervals to reflect how much of each group had already been sampled, even for the largest group, where we drew every work.” The first sentence gives the recipe but not what the interval shows. “Largest group” could mean the group with the most works rather than the group with the largest teams.
issues.fix: For each estimate, we used the middle 95% of the recalculated values as a range showing uncertainty from sampling. We did not narrow the range for groups where we sampled a large fraction of the list, even for the largest teams, where we sampled every listed work.

issues.problem: “Including works that scored zero because only their references were cited in the relevant window barely changed the main team-size result, though the appendix shows differences for the shorter window and for reviews compared with articles.” The reader has to consult the appendix to find out what changed.
issues.fix: Including works whose references were cited but whose own work was not barely changed the main team-size result. The estimated decline became steeper in the shorter window, but the difference between windows remained unclear. With these works included, the confidence interval for the difference between the article and review trends no longer included zero.

issues.problem: “We also compared each work’s average reference age using sampling weights.” The main text does not say how reference age was measured or distinguish this comparison clearly from the one that counts each reference separately.
issues.fix: We measured each reference’s age as the gap in publication years. We averaged those ages for each work, then compared the work averages using sampling weights.

issues.problem: “We also calculated each work’s share arriving in the publication year, counting citations through the second full calendar year. We compared works with negative and positive scores as if both groups had the same mix of publication years and quarters.” The denominator comes after the share, and it takes a moment to see that the quarters refer to when the works were published.
issues.fix: For each work, we counted citations from publication through the end of the second full calendar year and found the share that arrived in the publication year itself. We compared that share for works with negative and positive disruption scores, giving both groups the same mix of publication years and quarters for the comparison.

issues.problem: “Reviews and the model of highly cited references gave inconclusive results.” The summary does not say what the analysis could not determine in either case.
issues.fix: We could not tell whether disruption rank fell with team size for reviews, or whether the share of references at a given high citation count fell faster as that count rose for some team sizes than for others.

issues.problem: “The fitted share fell faster for ten-author than solo works.” The reader has to look back to identify the share and what made it fall.
issues.fix: In the model, each extra year in the age cutoff reduced the share of older references by a larger fraction for ten-author works than for solo works.

issues.problem: “The source excluded teams above 100 authors.” “The source” could mean OpenAlex itself or the list used for sampling.
issues.fix: The list we sampled from did not include works with more than 100 authors.
